How the estimate works

Resolution convention: r is a full spatial period (two detector samples). Require p ≤ r/2 and N ≥ ceil(πD/r). Angles are 0, 180/N, …, 180 − 180/N degrees; the endpoint is not duplicated.

q = Φ (p × 10⁻⁴)² η T   ·   L = −ln(T)
σ² = k² [F/(qt) + (σᵣ/(qt))²] / N + σ₀²
SNR = L / σ   ·   acquisition time = N(t + overhead)

q is transmitted detected counts per pixel per second. T and η are fractions. Ideal neutron counts are Poisson (F = 1); F ≥ 1 represents excess detector variance. σᵣ is independent read noise in equivalent detected counts per projection. Log-transmission variance uses first-order error propagation.

The reconstructed signal is a normalized attenuation proxy L. The empirical dimensionless gain k maps projection noise to this signal scale; it is not a universal tomography constant. Shared flat-field, drift and reconstruction errors are represented only by the non-averaging floor σ₀, in the same normalized attenuation units. Reference calibration image acquisition time is excluded.

For every integer N in the allowed range, solve the positive quadratic for the shortest exposure meeting the target; enforce exposure and count bounds, then minimize total time. Equal-time ties choose fewer projections. “Optimal” applies only to this bounded model.

Assumes uniform parallel-beam 180° coverage, a fully covered stationary sample, constant flux, independent views and representative transmission. No scatter, beam hardening, motion, detector MTF, saturation, cone-beam effects or spatially varying attenuation is simulated. Pixel sampling alone does not establish physical resolution. Calibrate and verify with representative phantoms before beamtime decisions.

Background: Kak & Slaney, Principles of Computerized Tomographic Imaging, chapters 3 and 5. The empirical SNR transfer equation here is an explicitly chosen planning model, not a claim from that reference.
